newsitem.title: SPAIN: FEATURE - Valencia sets itself ablaze in fiery fiesta.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Valencia sets itself ablaze in fiery fiesta.

text.p: Deafening blasts thunder through the streets, burning cinders fill the sky and one of Spain's most picturesque cities lies shrouded in smoke.

Every March, for six nights, the port of Valencia looks more like a war zone as citizens set their city alight during the "Fallas", a fiesta culminating in fireworks so loud that small children are kept away for fear their hearing could be damaged.
In a frenzy of pyrotechnics, flames and lavish processions, the city purges itself and welcomes the onset of spring as it has for centuries.

The festival of noise and fire reaches a climax on St Joseph's Day when more than 700 elaborate, larger-than-life caricatures known as "fallas" -- many depicting politicians and celebrities -- are burned to the ground.
With some figures set ablaze in narrow alleyways close to homes and buildings, the entire fire department of more than 300 are on hand to hose down facades and trees that catch fire.
The city echoes with resounding explosions. One of Valencia's biggest bank robberies took place during a Fallas fireworks display. Nobody noticed when the safe was blown up.
THE LOUDER, THE BETTER

Each year the grand finale -- known as the "crema", Spanish for cremation -- is marked by the burning of a massive effigy in the main square. This year, it was a 22-metre (72-feet) paper and plastic figure of a local mythical character.
More than 100,000 people crowded into the square to watch as the towering figure of an ancient warrior on horseback spat flames and rained burning embers down upon onlookers.
Tears trickled down the faces of the "falleras", the neighbourhood beauty contestants who preside over the burnings and compete for the title of "Queen of the Fallas".

The noise of fireworks fills the air day and night. At times spectators are cloaked in choking clouds of gunpowder smoke. "Valencians love noise, the louder the better," Judith Prosser, a local resident, said during the finale last Wednesday (March 19).

Pregnant women are told to stay away from the last, ear-splitting display, and small babies are kept at home. "No wonder the Valencians are deaf," Prosser shouts after the spectacle, her ears still ringing.
According to local lore, the festival dates back several hundred years and developed from craftsmen who used to set up wooden bases to hang oil lamps on winter nights.

With the advent of spring, they were no longer needed and were burned to the great delight of the workmen. Later, craftsmen started to dress the stands for fun and locals threw in bits of wood and old furniture to fuel the bonfire.
POLITICIANS MOCKED IN EFFIGY

Modern-day fallas -- from the Latin "facula", meaning torch -- are intricate works of art that gleefully poke fun at politicians, celebrities and local events. Creating them has become a highly competitive pastime.
Neighbourhoods rival one another to create the most lavish figures, and the shortlived monuments are shown off in Valencia's streets and squares during the fiesta.
"It's such a pity to see such beautiful works of art burned," Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman, one of the guests of honour who watched the show from the town hall, told journalists.
But artists are stoic about the fate of their creations.
"This is our job. We make money from doing this and we know exactly what is going to happen to the models in the end," said artist Manolo Mena, as he watched his labour turn to ashes.
Hundreds of artists toil year-round on their effigies.
Within each district, volunteers collect money from locals. Some of the more elaborate ones have attracted big corporate sponsorship.

This year's winner cost 17 million pesetas ($120,000) and depicted two huge figures in regal attire -- a Moor and a Christian, deadly enemies from centuries past -- holding glass mugs and toasting one another in a show of friendship.
Caricatures of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and top cabinet ministers riding camels decorated the base while other images satirised the news media's obsession with celebrities.
As the glowing cinders lay in small heaps and Valencia fell silent, artists prepared to start work on next year's creations.
"For the artists, this is a never-ending cycle," Mena said. ($1=142.5 Peseta)
